Aerius
ā-ē´rĭ-ŭs
n. (Aerius of Sebaste, fl. c. 360, presbyter of Pontus who taught that a bishop and a presbyter are of one order, rejected prayers and offerings for the dead, and refused fixed fasts; listed by Epiphanius among the heretics)
Greek Aerios, from aer, air. Known almost entirely from Epiphanius's Panarion, chapter 75.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Aerius was a presbyter and the manager of a hospice for the poor at Sebaste, a friend of the bishop Eustathius until a quarrel when Eustathius was preferred over him. He then taught three things that put him among the heretics in Epiphanius's catalogue. First, that a bishop differs in nothing from a presbyter, for Paul calls the same men elders and bishops: Titus was to “ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5), “For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God” (Tit 1:7), and Paul greets the church at Philippi “with the bishops and deacons” (Php 1:1), naming no third order. Second, that prayers and offerings for the dead are useless, since “it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27). Third, that fixed fasts and the Easter observance should not be imposed as law. His followers were driven from the churches and met in the fields. Epiphanius thought his first point madness. Jerome, who held a similar view of the original identity of bishop and presbyter, was never called a heretic for it. The Reformed churches, Presbyterian and Baptist alike, have since confessed what Aerius said on all three points.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines presbyter as an elder; a person somewhat advanced in age, who has authority in the church; a priest or minister.

expand to see more

PRESBYTER, n. In the primitive Christian church, an elder; a person somewhat advanced in age, who had authority in the church, and whose duty was to feed the flock over which the Holy Spirit had made him overseer.

2. A priest; one who has the pastoral or parochial charge.

Key Scripture

Tit 1:5 — "For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:"

Tit 1:7 — "For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;"

Php 1:1 — "Paul and Timotheus, the servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus which are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons:"

Heb 9:27 — "And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:"

Modern Corruption

Aerius was catalogued as a heretic for teaching what the New Testament plainly says about elders and bishops, and his case shows how early church custom was treated as apostolic law.

expand to see more

By the late fourth century the bishop had become a distinct and higher order over the presbyters, and prayers for the dead were universal. Epiphanius could not imagine that a presbyter who denied either was anything but a heretic. Yet the New Testament uses presbuteros and episkopos of the same men, and nowhere commands prayer for the departed. The equation of custom with apostolic tradition is the root of every later Roman claim.

The 1689 Confession confesses that the officers appointed by Christ for the church are bishops or elders, and deacons, and that prayer is to be made for the living, but not for the dead. Aerius's quarrel with his bishop may have sharpened his views, but the views themselves are the Bible's. The recovery is to test custom by Scripture, however ancient the custom.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek presbuteros (G4245), elder; episkopos (G1985), bishop, overseer; krisis (G2920), judgment.

expand to see more

Greek presbuteros (G4245) — elder; Titus 1:5.

Greek episkopos (G1985) — overseer, bishop; Titus 1:7, Philippians 1:1, Acts 20:28.

Greek krisis (G2920) — judgment; Hebrews 9:27.

Usage

"“ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) — elders and bishops one office."

"“with the bishops and deacons” (Php 1:1) — no third order at Philippi."

"“once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27) — against prayers for the dead."
